title: Path Sum
directAnswer: Walk root-to-leaf paths with DFS, subtracting each node's value from the target as you descend. At a leaf, return whether the remaining target equals exactly that leaf's value (equivalently, whether the running remainder hit zero). The trick is the leaf test: a node with no children is the only place you may declare success — never an internal node, never a null child.

remember.pattern: Root-to-leaf DFS with a shrinking remainder
remember.formula:
hasPathSum(node, target):
    if node is null: return false
    target -= node.val
    if node.left is null and node.right is null:
        return target == 0          # leaf: did we land exactly?
    return hasPathSum(node.left, target)
        or hasPathSum(node.right, target)
rules: Success is only declared at a **leaf** (both children null) — never at an internal node and never on a null child.
Subtract `node.val` from the target **on the way down**, then check `remainder == 0` at the leaf — don't accumulate and compare at the end unless you carry the sum explicitly.
A `null` node returns **false**, not true — an empty child is not a zero-length valid path.
Values can be **negative**, so you cannot prune a branch just because the remainder went negative.
Use **OR** across the two children — one valid path anywhere is enough to return true.
whenToUse: Asked whether ANY root-to-leaf path hits an exact target sum
You only need a yes/no answer, not the path itself
The path must start at the root and end at a leaf (not any node-to-node path)
Tree may contain negative values, ruling out greedy pruning
antiSignals: Need the actual list of paths → Path Sum II, collect the path then backtrack
Path may start/end anywhere, not root-to-leaf → Path Sum III or Max Path Sum (prefix sums / post-order)
Counting paths instead of existence → Path Sum III with a prefix-sum hash map
All values guaranteed positive AND you want to prune → still works, but the leaf check is what matters
remember.takeaway: Path Sum is the cleanest template for root-to-leaf DFS: push state (the remaining target) down the recursion and make the decision only at the leaf. Internalize the leaf guard and the null-returns-false rule, and the whole Path Sum family becomes variations on this single skeleton.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you correctly identify the leaf as the only valid place to succeed, handle null children as false, and propagate the shrinking remainder down the tree instead of trying to compare a total at the end.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning true at a node whose value alone equals the remaining target even though it still has children, or treating a null child as a valid zero-sum path — both falsely report success.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the leaf invariant explicitly ('I only check the sum where both children are null'), note that negative values forbid pruning, and offer the iterative stack variant carrying (node, remaining) pairs.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a binary tree and an integer `targetSum`, return `true` if the tree has a **root-to-leaf** path such that adding up all the values along the path equals `targetSum`.

A **leaf** is a node with no children.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000]
understanding: We are not asking whether the values sum to the target anywhere in the tree — we are asking specifically about a path that begins at the root and terminates at a leaf. Every node on that path contributes its value exactly once. The answer is a single boolean: does at least one such complete root-to-leaf path exist whose values add up to the target?

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the path have to end at a leaf, or can it stop at any node?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It must end at a leaf — a node with no children. Stopping at an internal node whose remainder happens to be zero is the classic wrong answer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can node values be negative?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, from -1000 to 1000. That means you cannot prune a branch when the remaining target goes negative — a later negative node could bring it back.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should an empty tree return?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: False. With no nodes there is no root-to-leaf path at all, so no path can sum to the target.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need the path itself or just whether one exists?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Just a boolean here. Returning the actual path is the follow-up, Path Sum II.

examples.explanation: The path 5 → 4 → 11 → 2 sums to 22 and ends at the leaf 2.
The two root-to-leaf paths are 1→2 (sum 3) and 1→3 (sum 4). Neither equals 5.
An empty tree has no root-to-leaf path, so even targetSum 0 returns false.

diagrams.title: Where you're allowed to declare success
diagrams.caption: The whole problem hinges on checking the sum only at leaves — the green nodes — never at internal nodes.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS with a Shrinking Remainder
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. Frame it as 'carry the remaining target down and decide only at a leaf' — that sentence captures the entire algorithm.
hints: You're looking for a path from root to a leaf. As you step into a child, how does the amount you still need to collect change?
Subtract the current node's value from the target before recursing. Then the question at each node becomes 'can the rest of the path make up the new remainder?'

The base of the recursion is the leaf: a node with no children succeeds only if the remaining target now equals that node's value (i.e., the remainder after subtracting hit zero). A null node is always false.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is visited at most once, so time is O(n). The recursion depth is the tree height h, giving O(h) stack space — O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree.
approaches.explanation:
The reframe that makes this trivial is to push state *down* the recursion. Instead of carrying an accumulating sum upward and comparing it at the end, we carry the *remaining* target downward. Each time we descend into a node we subtract that node's value from the target. The recursive question is then uniform at every node: *'starting here with this much left to collect, does a leaf-terminated path reach exactly zero?'*

**Why the decision belongs at the leaf and nowhere else.** The problem defines a valid path as root-to-*leaf*. So the only moment we are allowed to declare victory is when we stand on a node with no children — that is the end of a complete path. If we instead returned `true` the moment `remainder == node.val` at an internal node, we'd be accepting a path that stops in the middle of the tree, which the problem forbids. The leaf guard `node.left == null && node.right == null` is therefore not a performance tweak, it is the *definition* of correctness here.

**Why a null node must return false, not true.** It is tempting to write the base case as `if (node == null) return target == 0`. That is subtly wrong: consider a node with exactly one child and a remainder that happens to be zero. The missing child is a `null`, and if `null` returned `true` on a zero remainder, we'd falsely accept a path that never actually reached a leaf. Treating `null` as an unconditional `false` and putting the success test at the genuine leaf avoids this entire class of bug. The single-child case then correctly recurses only into the real child.

**Why we OR the two recursive calls.** We need *some* path to work, not all of them. So the result at an internal node is `leftSucceeds || rightSucceeds`. Short-circuit evaluation is a nice bonus — the instant the left subtree reports success, we never touch the right subtree. But the logical core is simply existential: one good path anywhere below is enough.

**Why negative values block pruning.** With all-positive values you could stop descending once the remainder dropped below the smallest possible future contribution. Here values range down to -1000, so a remainder of -7 today might be repaired by a -(-) ... actually by adding a negative node that pushes it back. Concretely, a later node of value -5 changes the remainder by subtracting -5, i.e. adding 5. Because the remainder can move in either direction, no early-exit pruning on its sign is safe — you must walk every root-to-leaf path until it ends.
approaches.insight: The state you propagate is the *remaining* target, not the accumulated sum. That single design choice — push the shrinking remainder down rather than bubble a total up — is what makes the leaf test a clean `remainder == 0` and generalizes directly to Path Sum II (carry the partial path too) and beyond.

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def hasPathSum(self, root: TreeNode, targetSum: int) -> bool:
    if root is None:                                  # no path here
        return False
    remaining = targetSum - root.val
    if root.left is None and root.right is None:      # leaf: the only place to decide
        return remaining == 0
    return (self.hasPathSum(root.left, remaining)
            or self.hasPathSum(root.right, remaining))  # one good path is enough

java.explanation: A null node is NOT a valid zero-length path — empty child means this branch failed, not succeeded.
Push state down: subtract this node's value so children inherit the smaller target to make up.
The leaf guard — both children null. This is the ONLY place we're permitted to declare a complete path.
At the leaf, success means the remainder hit exactly zero — the path's values summed to the original target.
OR the subtrees: one valid root-to-leaf path anywhere below is enough to return true.

python.explanation: Null node returns False — it is not a valid path terminus.
Carry the shrinking remainder downward instead of summing upward.

python.line: if root.left is None and root.right is None:
python.explanation: Leaf check — the sole valid place to evaluate the running sum.
Did the path land exactly on the target? Only meaningful at a leaf.
Existential OR — short-circuits the moment any path succeeds.

diagrams.title: The winning path 5 → 4 → 11 → 2
diagrams.caption: The highlighted spine sums to 22 and ends at a leaf; the remainder reaches 0 exactly at node 2.

edgeCases.behavior: Root is null → return false immediately. An empty tree has no root-to-leaf path.
Node 1 leaves remainder 0 but it is NOT a leaf (has child 2); recurse into 2 → remainder -1 at leaf → false. Demonstrates the leaf guard.
Negative values: -2 then -3 (a leaf) gives remainder 0 → true. Confirms pruning on sign would be wrong.

pitfalls: Writing the base case as `if (node == null) return target == 0` — falsely accepts a missing child as a valid path on a single-child node.
Returning true at an internal node when remainder == node.val, ignoring that the path must reach a leaf.
Pruning when the remainder goes negative — invalid because later nodes can be negative.
Forgetting the empty-tree case and dereferencing a null root.

approaches.name: Iterative DFS with an Explicit Stack
approaches.whenToMention: Offer when asked to avoid recursion or to preempt stack-overflow concerns on deep trees. Emphasize you push (node, remainingTarget) pairs.
hints: Recursion remembers, per call, which node you're at and how much target is left. To remove recursion, store those two facts yourself on a stack.
Push pairs of (node, remaining-after-this-node). Pop one, and if it's a leaf with remaining == 0, you've found a path.
For each non-leaf popped, push its non-null children with the remaining target reduced by the child's value.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every node is pushed and popped exactly once → O(n) time. The stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path's worth of nodes along the current DFS frontier, bounded by the height h → O(h) space.
approaches.explanation:
This is the same algorithm with the call stack made explicit, useful when the interviewer says 'no recursion' or when the tree could be deep enough to risk a stack overflow. The unit of state we save is a *pair*: a node and the target remaining *after* that node's value has been accounted for.

**Why store the remaining target alongside the node.** In the recursive version the remaining target lived in each stack frame as a parameter. Removing recursion means we must carry that same number ourselves. So each stack entry is `(node, remaining)` where `remaining` already has `node.val` subtracted out — the node arrives pre-credited, so the leaf test is again a clean `remaining == 0`.

**Why the leaf test is unchanged.** Correctness still depends on declaring success only at a genuine leaf. When we pop `(node, remaining)`, we check `node.left == null && node.right == null && remaining == 0`. If that holds, return `true` immediately. Otherwise we push whichever children exist, each with `remaining - child.val`. Null children are simply never pushed, which is the iterative analog of the recursive null-returns-false rule.

**Why a stack and not a queue.** Either works for an existence query, because we're not after the shortest or first path in any particular order — we just need *some* path. A stack gives depth-first behavior (dive down one path fully before backtracking), which tends to find a deep matching path with a smaller frontier; a queue would explore breadth-first. The choice doesn't affect correctness, only traversal order and peak memory shape.

**Why this matches recursion on complexity.** We touch each node once and the live frontier on the stack never exceeds the current path length, so time is O(n) and space is O(h) — identical to recursion, just with the bookkeeping moved off the language runtime and into our own container.
approaches.insight: The state you'd normally pass as a recursion parameter (the remaining target) becomes part of the stack entry. Recognizing 'a recursion parameter must become a tuple on my explicit stack' is the general recipe for converting any DFS to iterative form.

dryRun.intro: Stack holds (node, remaining). We push children with remaining reduced by the child's value; success needs a leaf with remaining 0.

java.explanation: Seed the node stack with the root; its paired remaining is pushed in lockstep.
Store the target already reduced by the root's value, so leaf checks stay a clean rem == 0.
Leaf AND zero remainder — the iterative form of the recursive leaf guard.
Children inherit the remainder minus their own value, mirroring the downward subtraction in recursion.

python.explanation: Each entry pairs a node with the remaining target after that node — the state recursion kept in a frame.
Unpack the saved pair; rem already excludes node.val.

python.line: if node.left is None and node.right is None and rem == 0:
python.explanation: Success only at a true leaf with the remainder exhausted to zero.
Push only real children, each crediting its value — null children are skipped, matching null-returns-false.

edgeCases.behavior: Push (1,0); pop it, it's a leaf with rem 0 → return true.
Push (1,0); pop — node 1 is NOT a leaf (has child 2), so no match; push (2,-1); leaf with rem -1 → false.
Explicit stack avoids recursion depth limits; O(h) frontier handles it where recursion might overflow.

pitfalls: Checking rem == 0 without also confirming the node is a leaf — accepts mid-path stops.
Pushing null children onto the stack, then dereferencing them later.
Forgetting to subtract the child's value when pushing, so the remainder never shrinks correctly.
Mismatching the two parallel stacks (node vs remaining) by pushing to one but not the other.

commonMistakes: Declaring success at an internal node instead of only at a leaf.
Writing the base case as `node == null → target == 0`, which accepts missing children as valid paths.
Pruning a branch when the remainder turns negative, despite negative node values.
Returning true for an empty tree when targetSum is 0.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Treating a null child as a valid zero-sum path
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Putting the success test on the null base case means a single-child node whose remainder is zero falsely succeeds through its missing child, even though no leaf was reached.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Succeeding at an internal node
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The path must end at a leaf. Returning true the moment the remainder equals the node value ignores that the node still has children, accepting an illegal mid-tree stop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Pruning on a negative remainder
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With positive-only values you could stop when the remainder went negative, but here values reach -1000, so a negative remainder can still be corrected by a later negative node.

followupVariations.title: Path Sum II
followupVariations.hint: Return every root-to-leaf path that sums to target — carry the partial path and backtrack on the way up.

followupVariations.title: Path Sum III
followupVariations.hint: Count paths that may start and end anywhere — prefix-sum hash map of running sums.

followupVariations.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
followupVariations.hint: Any node-to-node path; post-order returning the best downward arm at each node.

followupVariations.title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
followupVariations.hint: Same root-to-leaf DFS, but build a number digit-by-digit instead of testing a sum.

patternNote: Root-to-leaf DFS carrying state downward. Recognise it whenever a property is defined over complete paths from the root to a leaf. The skeleton — null returns the failure value, decide at the leaf, OR/aggregate over children — underlies Sum Root to Leaf Numbers, Path Sum II, and Binary Tree Paths.
